name: Osteogenesis Imperfecta

diagnosticCriteria.formalCriteriaName: Sillence Classification (revised and expanded); Nosology of the International Skeletal Dysplasia Society

criteria.description: Recurrent fractures with minimal or no trauma
Family history consistent with autosomal dominant (COL1A1/COL1A2) or autosomal recessive inheritance

diagnosticCriteria.minimumForDiagnosis: Clinical diagnosis based on recurrent low-trauma fractures plus supportive features. Genetic testing for COL1A1/COL1A2 or rarer genes (IFITM5, SERPINF1, CRTAP, etc.) confirms diagnosis.
diagnosticCriteria.notes: OI is classified into multiple types (historically I-IV by Sillence, now >20 genetic types). Severity ranges from mild (Type I) to perinatally lethal (Type II).

pathognomonic.symptomName: Recurrent fractures with minimal or no trauma
pathognomonic.notes: Hallmark feature; fracture frequency varies by type

common.notes: Most pronounced in Type I; may darken with age
More severe in Types III and IV
Opalescent, translucent, and fragile teeth; more common in Types III and IV

occasional.notes: Mixed conductive and sensorineural; onset typically in 2nd-3rd decade
More common in severe types (III, IV)

rare.notes: Can cause brainstem compression; more common in severe types

rare.symptomName: Cardiopulmonary complications (valvular disease, restrictive lung disease)

laboratory: Bone turnover markers may be abnormal (elevated alkaline phosphatase during fractures)
DEXA scan shows reduced bone mineral density
Type I procollagen analysis on fibroblasts (historical)
imaging: Skeletal radiographs showing osteopenia, fractures in various stages of healing
Bowing and deformity of long bones
Vertebral compression fractures on spine imaging
DEXA scan for bone density quantification
genetic: COL1A1 mutations (most common, ~70-80% of OI cases; quantitative defects in Type I)
IFITM5 mutations (OI Type V, with hyperplastic callus)
Autosomal recessive genes: CRTAP, LEPRE1/P3H1, PPIB, SERPINF1, SERPINH1, BMP1, WNT1, TMEM38B, SPARC, etc.
Autosomal dominant in most cases; recessive forms account for 5-10%
other: Clinical assessment of fracture history and family pedigree

distinguishingFeatures: cEDS has marked skin hyperextensibility (absent in OI)
OI has bone fragility as primary feature
Some overlap with rare COL1A1 variants
Marfan features tall stature (OI often short stature)
Marfan has aortic root dilation and ectopia lentis
OI has bone fragility and fractures

redFlags: Multiple fractures in infancy or childhood (must distinguish from non-accidental injury)
Basilar invagination symptoms (headache, dysphagia, cranial nerve palsies, myelopathy)
Blue sclerae alone is insufficient - many infants have blue sclerae normally
Fractures with no trauma or minimal trauma across different stages of healing
references: Marini JC, et al. Osteogenesis imperfecta. Nat Rev Dis Primers. 2017;3:17052.
Sillence DO, Senn A, Danks DM. Genetic heterogeneity in osteogenesis imperfecta. J Med Genet. 1979;16(2):101-16.
Forlino A, Marini JC. Osteogenesis imperfecta. Lancet. 2016;387(10028):1657-71.
Rauch F, Glorieux FH. Osteogenesis imperfecta. Lancet. 2004;363(9418):1377-85.
